title: The Prisoner Who Became President
shortDescription: Born into a royal Thembu family in a South African village, Nelson Mandela was stripped of privilege, became a lawyer, and gave up nearly three decades of his life in prison to end apartheid — then walked out to lead the country he had been jailed for freeing as its first Black president.
introduction: On 18 July 1918, in the village of Mvezo in the Eastern Cape of South Africa, a boy was born to a chief who was about to lose everything. He was named Rolihlahla, a Xhosa word that means "troublemaker." He would grow up herding cattle in a rural homeland, study law in the segregated cities of Johannesburg, and spend twenty-seven years in prison for fighting the apartheid regime — the system of racial separation that ruled his country. When he walked free at seventy-one in 1990, he did not return bitterness. Four years later he became South Africa's first Black president, and the world came to call him Madiba.

chapters.heading: A boy in the Transkei hills
paragraphs: Nelson Mandela was born Rolihlahla Mandela on 18 July 1918 in Mvezo, a small village on the banks of the Mbashe River in the Transkei, a region of rolling green hills on the southeast coast of what was then the Union of South Africa. His father, Gadla Henry Mphakanyiswa Mandela, was a chief and a trusted counsellor to the royal house of the Thembu people, a Xhosa-speaking nation that had lived in the region for centuries. His mother, Nosekeni Fanny, was the chief's third wife. The name his parents gave him, Rolihlahla, is a Xhosa phrase that means 'pulling the branch of a tree' — spoken loosely, it means 'troublemaker.' Decades later he would become famous under two other names: Nelson, the English name a schoolteacher gave him, and Madiba, the clan name by which South Africans came to know him with affection.

When Rolihlahla was a small boy, his father fell into a dispute with a white magistrate over a matter of tribal cattle. Gadla refused to obey the magistrate's summons, and in 1926 the colonial government stripped him of his chieftainship, his land, and his cattle. The family was forced out of Mvezo and moved to Qunu, a smaller village nearby, where the boy herded sheep and calves, played with other village children along the dusty tracks, and learned the customs of his people. He would later remember these early years with warmth — the games, the herdboys, the open sky — even though the family was poorer than before. His mother, he recalled, was a deeply devout Christian who sent him to a local Methodist mission school when he was about seven. It was there that a teacher named Miss Mdingane gave him the English name the world would use ever after.

In about 1930, when Rolihlahla was twelve, his father died of a lung disease, and the boy's life changed for a second time. His mother took him to the Great Place at Mqhekezweni, the royal court of the Thembu regent, Chief Jongintaba Dalindyebo, who had been his father's friend and had agreed to raise the child as his own. At the Great Place, the young Mandela was brought up alongside the regent's own children and groomed for a future as a royal counsellor. He attended the mission school next to the palace, walked with the chief, and listened late into the night to the stories the elders told — including the grief of his people when the colonial wars of the nineteenth century had destroyed their kingdom. He would say later that the seeds of his lifelong anger at injustice were planted in those fireside hours.

media.alt: Rolling hills and scattered homes of the village of Qunu in the Eastern Cape, where Mandela spent his boyhood
media.caption: The hills of Qunu, the Eastern Cape village where Mandela herded cattle as a boy.

chapters.heading: Clarkebury to Fort Hare
paragraphs: At sixteen, Mandela underwent the traditional Xhosa ceremony of initiation into manhood, and the elders gave him the new name Dalibunga. He had already shown himself to be an outstanding student. In 1934 he entered Clarkebury, a Methodist boarding school in the district of Engcobo, where he earned his Junior Certificate in two years instead of the usual three. In 1937 he moved on to Healdtown, the Wesleyan college at Fort Beaufort — the largest school for Black students in the country at the time — where some of the best-known royal families of the region sent their sons. At Healdtown he read, debated, ran long distances, and learned to box. When he matriculated in 1938, he was one of a very small number of Black South Africans who had finished high school, and he had made his first friend from outside his own language group, a Sotho speaker who broadened his world.

In 1939, with the regent's support, Mandela enrolled at the University College of Fort Hare near Alice, the only residential university for Black students in South Africa at that time. Fort Hare was small — about a hundred and fifty students — but it was extraordinary. Some of the most gifted young Black minds of the country studied there, and it was there that Mandela met a fellow student from the Eastern Cape named Oliver Tambo. The two young men would become law partners, fellow prisoners of the struggle, and lifelong friends. At Fort Hare, Mandela joined the Student Christian Association, performed in a drama society play about Abraham Lincoln, and threw himself into campus life. Then, at the end of his first year, he became caught up in a student boycott of the university's food, and was expelled for refusing to accept a deal that he thought betrayed the other students. He never returned to Fort Hare as a student.

Back at the Great Place, the regent had quietly arranged two marriages for him and for his own son, Justice. Mandela, now nineteen and with no desire to be married to someone chosen for him, made a decision that would cost him his place in the Thembu royal world. He and Justice gathered some of the regent's cattle, sold them for money, and fled by train to Johannesburg, nearly three hundred miles away. In the city he found work — first as a night watchman at Crown Mines, then as a clerk — and by a stroke of fortune he met a young activist named Walter Sisulu, who took the country boy under his wing. Sisulu found Mandela a place as an articled clerk at a white law firm, an exceedingly rare opportunity for a Black man in the 1940s, and introduced him to the circles where the future Black leadership of South Africa was being made.

media.alt: Buildings on the campus of the University of Fort Hare in the Eastern Cape
media.caption: The University of Fort Hare, the only residential university for Black students in South Africa when Mandela enrolled in 1939.

chapters.heading: The making of a freedom fighter
paragraphs: While Mandela was studying for his Bachelor of Arts degree through the University of South Africa and preparing for an LLB at the University of the Witwatersrand, a critical thing happened in South African politics: in 1948 the all-white National Party won power and built the legal machinery of apartheid. The word apartheid is Afrikaans for 'apartness,' and the system was exactly that — a vast body of laws that classified the people of South Africa by race and reserved power, land, and opportunity to whites. Black South Africans, the overwhelming majority of the population, could not vote, could not own land in most of the country, could not marry across the colour line, could not live or work where they chose, and were forced to carry passbooks that controlled their every move. It was against this machine that Nelson Mandela would spend his life.

Mandela had joined the African National Congress (ANC), the country's main Black liberation movement, in 1943, and in 1944 he was one of the founders of its Youth League, together with Walter Sisulu, Oliver Tambo, and the young visionary Anton Lembede. The Youth League was impatient with the older leaders' patience, and insisted that the ANC should demand full rights for all South Africans now. When the National Party declared apartheid in 1948, Mandela and his comrades were ready. In 1952 he was a leading organiser of the Defiance Campaign, in which thousands of volunteers deliberately broke apartheid's unjust laws and filled the prisons in a Gandhian campaign of civil disobedience. He was arrested, convicted, and given a suspended sentence, and was soon one of the most banned men in the country — forbidden by court order from attending gatherings, leaving his town without permission, or even speaking to more than a handful of people at a time.

Banning orders could not stop him. In December 1952, Mandela and Oliver Tambo opened the first Black-owned law firm in Johannesburg. Their offices were never short of clients: Black South Africans, refused help by white lawyers, came in streams with cases about passes, evictions, and the daily humiliations of apartheid. The firm became a living protest. In 1956 Mandela was arrested with more than a hundred other leaders and charged with high treason in a spectacle of a trial that dragged on for four and a half years — and that ended in 1961 with every accused acquitted. Yet the government was preparing harsher weapons. On 21 March 1960, at Sharpeville, police fired into a crowd of unarmed protesters and killed sixty-nine people. The massacre moved the country, the violence reached even the most patient, and the ANC was banned outright. Mandela, returning to its cause with his passport of hope burned to nothing, came to a hard conclusion: if the movement was to survive, it had to be prepared to strike back.

media.alt: Nelson Mandela and others at a protest in 1960, burning their passbooks
media.caption: Mandela and fellow protesters burn their passbooks in 1960, resisting the law that governed every movement of Black South Africans.

chapters.heading: The Spear of the Nation
paragraphs: In 1961, after decades of peaceful protest had been answered with bullets and bans, Mandela and his comrades founded a new armed wing of the liberation movement and named it Umkhonto we Sizwe — the Spear of the Nation. Mandela was its commander-in-chief. The organisation's strategy was careful and unromantic: it would sabotage government installations — power pylons, railways, government offices — choosing targets that crippled the state rather than people, and steering clear of civilian lives. The goal was not to win a war, which Mandela knew was impossible, but to force the government to negotiate. In a statement at the time he was clear-eyed: 'We do not wish to see the Velvet glove of the government slip to reveal the iron fist, not because we fear it, but because we know it will not solve the conflict.' He had already been underground for more than a year, slipping between secret houses, moving like a shadow through the country he was preparing to fight.

In January 1962, Mandela left South Africa secretly to travel through Africa and Europe, raising support and receiving military training for the new army. He visited newly independent African nations, met leaders, and saw with his own eyes a continent throwing off colonial rule. On 5 August 1962, just after he had returned home, he was arrested at a roadblock near the town of Howick, disguised as a chauffeur. He was tried in Pretoria, convicted of incitement and of leaving the country illegally, and sentenced to five years in prison. While he served that sentence, the police raided the underground headquarters of the movement at Lilliesleaf Farm in Rivonia, near Johannesburg, and found papers that linked Mandela and nine colleagues to plans for an armed uprising. In October 1963 the government put all of them on trial for sabotage and conspiracy to overthrow the state.

The trial that followed — the Rivonia Trial — became the most famous political trial in the history of the continent. Mandela and his comrades faced the real possibility of the death sentence. On 20 April 1964, Mandela stood in the dock in Pretoria's Palace of Justice and announced that he would not give evidence from the witness box, choosing instead to give a statement of his own. He admitted to the court that he had helped found Umkhonto we Sizwe and had prepared sabotage with it. Then he gave the reason. 'I have cherished the ideal of a democratic and free society in which all persons live together in harmony and with equal opportunities,' he said. 'It is an ideal which I hope to live for and to achieve. But if needs be, it is an ideal for which I am prepared to die.' On 12 June 1964, all but two of the accused were sentenced to life imprisonment. Mandela was forty-five years old. That night he was flown, under cover of darkness, to the prison island where he would spend most of the next twenty-seven years.

chapters.heading: Robben Island, the island prison
paragraphs: Robben Island lies a few miles offshore from Cape Town, a low, windswept slab of rock in the cold Atlantic. For centuries the country had sent its unwanted there: lepers, the sick, and finally its most dangerous political prisoners. From 1964, Mandela was among them, prisoner number 466/64. The island prison was built to break men. The prisoners were made to break rock and work in a glare of blinding white lime in the quarry, which wrecked Mandela's eyesight permanently. They were issued short trousers and sandals instead of long pants and shoes, a deliberate humiliation. They were allowed one letter and one visit every six months, and the letters were censored so heavily that prisoners wrote about the weather and the price of bread, in the hope that something of meaning might pass. 'When I walked into that prison,' Mandela later said, 'I had to leave my bitterness behind. You have to adapt or die physically and spiritually.'

The prison years took an enormous personal toll. In 1968 Mandela's mother died, and in 1969 his eldest son, Thembi, was killed in a car crash; the authorities refused him permission to attend either funeral. His marriage to Evelyn Mase had long since ended, and while he was in prison he married a second time, in 1958, to a young social worker from Bizana named Winnie Madikizela, who became his own partner in the struggle and paid for it with bans, house arrest, and imprisonment herself. Mandela saw almost none of his children grow up. Yet inside the walls he refused the prison's terms. He studied for an LLB through the University of London and, decades later, earned it through the University of South Africa even while jailed. He learned Afrikaans, the language of his jailers, so that he could speak to them as people. He read, he exercised, he took up gardening in a small plot he was given, and he organised his fellow prisoners into schools of learning and debate.

The government tried, over the years, to set him free on conditions he would not accept. In 1976 the Minister of Prisons offered to release him if he would recognise the independence of the Transkei and go to live there; Mandela refused. In 1985 President P.W. Botha offered freedom if he would renounce violence and the armed struggle. His daughter Zindzi read his answer to a crowd in Soweto: 'Only free men can negotiate. Prisoners cannot enter into contracts.' As his freedom was refused, his legend grew. Around the world, in cities he had never seen, young people wore T-shirts demanding the release of a prisoner they had never met, and the movement that gathered behind his name became one of the most powerful international campaigns of the twentieth century. In 1982 he was moved to Pollsmoor Prison on the mainland, and in December 1988 to a cottage at Victor Verster Prison near Paarl, where the government kept him in comfort to soften him for what it knew was coming.

media.alt: The narrow prison cell on Robben Island where Nelson Mandela spent eighteen years
media.caption: Mandela's cell on Robben Island, where he was held from 1964 until 1982 — eight hours of quarry labour a day, one letter every six months.

chapters.heading: The long walk to freedom
paragraphs: By the late 1980s, the single most recognisable prisoner on Earth had become the single most powerful symbol of everything the world hated about apartheid. The South African government was cornered: sanctions were biting, the economy was struggling, and the country was on the edge of a racial civil war. In 1989 a new state president, F.W. de Klerk, concluded that apartheid could not be defended any longer. On 2 February 1990, in a speech to parliament, he announced the unbanning of the African National Congress and other liberation movements. Nine days later, on 11 February 1990, at five in the afternoon, Nelson Mandela walked out of Victor Verster Prison holding the hand of his wife, Winnie. He was seventy-one years old. He had been in prison for twenty-seven years. Across the world, cameras captured one image: an old man, tall and grey, walking into the open air, smiling.

Mandela emerged with his cause intact and his anger in check. That evening he addressed a crowd of fifty thousand people from the balcony of Cape Town City Hall and repeated his central demand: democracy for all, and an end to white-minority rule. Then he set about the hardest negotiation of his life. Over the next four years he led the ANC's side in talks with the government and his opponent-turned-partner, President de Klerk, through the most dangerous period the country had known. Extremists on both sides tried to derail the peace — in April 1993 the charismatic young leader Chris Hani was assassinated, and Mandela calmed a nation poised to explode by addressing the country on television with a sternness and authority that stopped the violence. In December 1993, Mandela and de Klerk were jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for their work in ending apartheid. 'A nation should not be judged by how it treats its highest citizens,' he told a world audience, 'but its lowest ones.'

On 27 April 1994, South Africa held its first election in which every adult — of every race — could vote. More than nineteen million people went to the polls, many standing in queues for hours, some for the first time in their lives, in almost every case for the only time. The ANC won a sweeping victory, with about sixty-three per cent of the vote. Parliament elected Nelson Mandela the country's president. On 10 May 1994, before four thousand guests and a billion viewers, he was inaugurated at the Union Buildings in Pretoria, the seat of the government that had jailed him. He had spent a quarter of a century of his life behind bars for the right to stand on that lawn. 'Out of the experience of an extraordinary human disaster that lasted too long,' he said, 'must be born a society of which all humanity will be proud.' South Africa, he promised, was at last a rainbow nation, at peace with itself and the world.

chapters.heading: One term, and a legacy for the ages
paragraphs: Mandela governed for only five years, 1994 to 1999, and he used the time to build a country, not a following. He took a formerly all-white administration and turned it into a Government of National Unity, appointing F.W. de Klerk as one of his deputy presidents. He shared his old allies — the defence officials, the rugby players, even the prosecutor who had sent him to prison — the same generosity he had practiced in the courtroom in 1964. He travelled to lunch with the widow of Hendrik Verwoerd, the architect of apartheid, and he wore the green jersey of the national rugby team, long the symbol of white supremacy, when South Africa hosted and won the Rugby World Cup in 1995. The single most famous gesture of his presidency came when he placed the apartheid system's own history on trial instead of its people: the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, invited victims and perpetrators to testify and offered amnesty for full confession. The country chose memory over revenge.

Under Mandela, South Africa wrote itself a new constitution with a bill of rights at its heart, including protections for minorities and freedoms of expression and conscience. His government brought 1.5 million children into the education system, extended electricity and water to millions of households that had never had them, and created free healthcare for pregnant women and young children. Then, at the peak of his authority, in 1999 he did what almost no African leader of his era did: he handed power to his chosen successor, Thabo Mbeki, and walked away willingly. His decision to leave was itself one of the great gifts to his country — it proved that the new South Africa would not be the prisoner of one man, however beloved. He retired to his home village of Qunu, the boyhood landscape of his early years.

Mandela spent his last decade the way he had spent his first: at work. Through the Nelson Mandela Foundation, he campaigned against poverty and for children, quietly raising money by inviting the wealthy to walk with him through Africa's shantytowns. He helped broker the Arusha peace agreement that ended the civil war in Burundi. He spoke out, finally, on HIV/AIDS — in 2005 he publicly announced that his own son Makgatho had died of AIDS, forcing the stigma of the disease out into the open. In 2009 the United Nations declared his birthday, 18 July, Nelson Mandela International Day, calling on people everywhere to give sixty-seven minutes of their time to service, one minute for every year he had given to his people. Nelson Mandela died at his home in Johannesburg on 5 December 2013, aged ninety-five, and was buried in the Qunu hills where the herdboy had once run. His own words, written long before, are the truest epitaph: 'It always seems impossible until it is done.'
